All Permutations

CountingAlgorithmsSequences

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Explore all the ways to order the numbers 1 to N, written also as cycles.
How to play: Change N or pick one of the three generators, R, L or H, and watch the rows change order.

Numbers N 3
Look for the math

There are n! ways to order n objects. Three different algorithms can list them all, and each gives the same set of rows in a different order.

Three generators

R is a short recursion: put the next unused number in each position and try again. L starts at 1, 2, …, n and repeatedly finds the first position from the right that can be increased, then reverses the tail — this is Dijkstra's next-permutation step. H is Heap's algorithm, which recurses and swaps either the first or the last element depending on the parity of the current size. The logic test transcribes all three and compares them row for row on every n up to 7.

Cycles and derangements

Each row is also written as a product of cycles: follow 1 to its image, then that number to its image, until it returns. For n = 3 the six rows are the rigid motions of a triangle — two rotations and three reflections plus the identity. A permutation with no fixed point is a derangement; the number of them satisfies D(n) = (n−1)(D(n−1) + D(n−2)), which the logic test checks against the listed rows.

What the check found

All three generators produce exactly n! distinct rows, in their own characteristic order, for every n up to 8. The recursion in the original applet prints the numbers 2 to N+1 (an off-by-one); this port keeps its exact order but shows 1 to N, as the page states. The browser draws at most a thousand rows and reports the true count.

Set N to 4 and compare the first ten rows under R, L and H. Does any row appear twice?
